requirements.requirement: Keep the installed curl package at its current version when updates are performed.
requirements.summary: curl began at 0:7.76.1-40.el9 while 0:7.76.1-40.el9_8.7 was available. A version lock for the installed release was added, and actual targeted upgrade attempts before and after reboot did nothing and left the installed version unchanged.

requirements.requirement: Preserve the installed operating-system release and kernel, using software compatible with the legacy RHEL 9 platform.
requirements.summary: The node remained on RHEL 9.8 and running kernel 5.14.0-687.20.1.el9_8 before and after the work and reboot. The required version-lock plugin was installed from an EL9 repository as an EL9 package.

overall_summary: Both material task outcomes are satisfied. The curl version lock was directly exercised against a newer available build and persisted across reboot. RHEL 9.8 and the original kernel were preserved. The mandatory restart protocol is strong: it records healthy pre-restart state, acknowledged reboot scheduling, a changed boot identity, restored curl functionality and lock behavior, and matching lifecycle boot-identity observations.
limitations: No full system-wide update was executed; update protection was demonstrated with targeted `dnf upgrade curl` attempts against a directly observed newer candidate.

The restart evidence contains no separate application data or cluster-state probe because this is a single-node package-management task with no task-specific application data or cluster service. Package state, executable functionality, platform state, and package-manager health were recovered and observed.

operational_hygiene.summary: No unnecessary mutations were identified. Installing the version-lock plugin and adding the curl lock directly implemented the task; the update attempts were bounded verification and reported no package changes; and the scheduled reboot was required by the provider-wide restart protocol. Post-execution observations show healthy package state, no failed services, no new exposure, and only expected reboot-related process and temporary-directory identity changes. The transient reboot unit left no observed failure or residue.
